sender.en: Someone you met on Facebook, a dating app or Messenger who says they are a successful professional working overseas

name.en: Love scam: an online partner overseas who needs money for fees

how.en: Someone you meet on social media or a dating app, often claiming to be a business executive, engineer or doctor based overseas, builds a close relationship over weeks of messages. Then a problem comes up: legal fees, a cheque or parcel that has to be released, or an emergency, and they ask you to transfer money, promising to pay you back with more. The requests continue after each payment. Police recorded 100 love scam cases with RM3.5 million lost in January 2026 alone; 60 per cent of victims are women and 72 per cent are aged 30 to 50.

text.en: A friendly stranger contacts you on Facebook, Messenger or a dating app, and may move the chat to WhatsApp.
They say they are a successful professional overseas and talk about a future together.
A problem comes up: legal fees, a cheque or parcel to release, or an emergency.
They ask you to transfer money to accounts they give, promising to repay you, and keep asking.

My dear, I am so sorry to ask you this. The lawyer says I must pay the legal fee before they release the cheque for the project. My accounts are frozen here. Can you help me with RM15,000 today? Once it clears I will return double to you, I promise.

Someone you have never met in person asking for money.
A professional overseas who cannot use their own bank account.
Promises to pay you back many times over once a fee is paid.
Payments to different accounts that are not in their name.
Never send money to someone you have only met online.
Check the accounts and phone numbers they give on Semak Mule, and talk to family or friends.
If you have already paid, call 997 and your bank straight away, then make a police report.

Senior citizen loses nearly RM200k in love scam involving fake corporate figure

story.en: A 70-year-old retired government employee in Muar met two people on Facebook Messenger who said they were a corporate executive and a specialist doctor based overseas. They said they needed help with legal fees linked to a construction contract and the release of a US$85,000 cheque, and promised her money once it was done. She made eight transfers totalling RM183,100 from her savings, and they kept asking for more.
